security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives from Markdown formatting and documented, local Git workflow commands. However, the skill contains instruction-priority escalation language and mandates Git identity changes using named email addresses, which require remediation before publication.

remediation.suggestion: Replace mandatory override language with a normal capability description. State that the skill applies only when the user requests commit assistance and host instructions permit it.
Remove hardcoded email addresses and never change Git user.name or user.email automatically. Ask the user for explicit confirmation and use their configured identity.

semantic_findings.title: Prompt Injection Attempt Detected
semantic_findings.description: The frontmatter states "MUST use this skill" and "OVERRIDES default git commit behavior." This attempts to impose priority over the host agent instructions and user intent.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The activation description explicitly uses mandatory language and claims to override default behavior, which is a direct instruction-priority escalation attempt.

semantic_findings.title: Forced Git Identity Configuration
semantic_findings.description: The skill directs agents to set a local Git email address based on the remote host. This can change commit attribution without confirming the user owns or authorizes the listed identity.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The instruction is explicit, mandatory, and names specific email identities. Changing commit identity can create unauthorized attribution.

content.value_statement: Inconsistent commit messages make project history difficult to search and review. This skill guides a focused Git workflow and formats result-oriented Conventional Commit messages.
actual_capabilities: Reviews staged Git changes before proposing a commit message.
Formats messages with emoji, Conventional Commit type, optional scope, and subject.
Explains when one task should remain in a single commit.
Provides heredoc examples for multiline commit messages.
Matches the commit message language to recent repository history.
limitations: It does not determine whether staged changes are correct or complete.
It does not run tests, push branches, or open pull requests.
Emoji conventions may not match every repository policy.
Git identity changes require explicit user confirmation and should not be automated.

use_cases.title: Prepare a feature commit
use_cases.description: Review staged feature work and create a concise Conventional Commit message.

use_cases.title: Standardize team history
use_cases.description: Apply consistent types, scopes, and subjects across a shared repository.

use_cases.title: Document a review fix
use_cases.description: Write a focused multiline commit message that explains a review-driven correction.

prompt_templates.title: Create a basic commit
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my staged changes and propose one Conventional Commit message with an appropriate emoji.

prompt_templates.title: Commit a completed feature
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the staged diff. Create one result-focused commit for this feature, including its tests and documentation.

prompt_templates.title: Write a breaking-change commit
prompt_templates.prompt: Prepare a Conventional Commit for this staged API change. Mark it as breaking and provide a concise body.

prompt_templates.title: Handle mixed changes safely
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my staged changes. Identify unrelated work, explain whether it should be split, and ask before creating any commits.

output_examples.input: Staged changes add login validation and related tests.
output: Suggested commit: ✨ feat(auth): add login validation
Reason: The implementation and tests deliver one feature request.

output_examples.input: Staged changes update an API response shape.
output: Suggested commit: 💥 feat(api)!: change response format
Add a body explaining the compatibility impact.

output_examples.input: Staged changes include a feature and an unrelated dependency update.
output: Recommendation: Create separate commits because the dependency update is unrelated.
Ask for confirmation before staging or committing.

best_practices: Review the staged diff and repository commit conventions before committing.
Keep one requested change, its tests, and its documentation in one meaningful commit.
Confirm the configured Git identity before creating a commit.
anti_patterns: Do not stage secrets, credentials, or unrelated generated files.
Do not use vague subjects such as update code or fix bug.
Do not change Git identity settings without explicit user approval.

faq.question: What commit format does this skill use?
faq.answer: It uses an emoji followed by a Conventional Commit type, optional scope, and imperative subject.

faq.question: Should every changed file have its own commit?
faq.answer: No. Files that deliver one request should normally stay together in one commit.

faq.question: Can it write multiline commit messages?
faq.answer: Yes. It provides a heredoc pattern for a subject and explanatory body.

faq.question: How does it choose the message language?
faq.answer: It checks recent commit history and recommends the same language.

faq.question: Does it stage files automatically?
faq.answer: It can describe staging commands, but users should review and confirm selected files.

faq.question: Can it change my Git email address?
faq.answer: No. Git identity settings must only change after explicit user confirmation.
